PACE propagates evidence over a structured skill graph to accelerate diagnostic coverage and applies contextual bandits to select scenarios that target gaps the trainee is prepared to address. Empirical results show that PACE achieves 19.50% faster time-to-competence and 10.95% higher terminal mastery compared to state-of-the-art frameworks. Co-pilot studies with practicing training officers further demonstrate a 95.45% alignment rate between PACE's and experts' pedagogical judgments on real-world cases. Under estimation, PACE cuts turnaround time to merely 34 seconds from 11.58 minutes, up to 95.08% reduction.

AI.tldr: PACE is a personalized adaptive curriculum engine for 9-1-1 call-taker training that uses probabilistic skill modeling and contextual bandits to recommend training scenarios, achieving 19.5% faster competence and 10.95% higher mastery compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: 9-1-1 call-taking training involves mastering over a thousand interdependent skills, but nationwide labor shortages strain training capacity. Current practice cannot scale the personalization needed to tailor training to each trainee's evolving competencies, creating a significant burden for trainers.
AI.method: PACE maintains probabilistic beliefs over trainee skill states, models individual learning and forgetting dynamics, and recommends training scenarios balancing new competency acquisition with existing skill retention. It propagates evidence over a structured skill graph for faster diagnostic coverage and uses contextual bandits to select scenarios targeting gaps the trainee is prepared to address.
AI.result: PACE achieves 19.50% faster time-to-competence and 10.95% higher terminal mastery compared to state-of-the-art frameworks. Co-pilot studies show 95.45% alignment between PACE's and experts' pedagogical judgments. Under estimation, PACE reduces turnaround time from 11.58 minutes to 34 seconds (95.08% reduction).
AI.conclusion: PACE effectively addresses the scalability challenge in 9-1-1 call-taker training by augmenting trainer decision-making with personalized adaptive curriculum recommendations, significantly improving training efficiency and outcomes while maintaining strong alignment with expert pedagogical judgment.

title: Legal interpretation and AI: from expert systems to argumentation and LLMs
summary: AI and Law research has encountered legal interpretation in different ways, in the context of its evolving approaches and methodologies. Research on expert system has focused on legal knowledge engineering, with the goal of ensuring that human-generated interpretations can be precisely transferred into knowledge-bases, to be consistently applied. Research on argumentation has aimed at representing the structure of interpretive arguments, as well as their dialectical interactions, to assess of the acceptability of interpretive claims within argumentation frameworks. Research on machine learning has focused on the automated generation of interpretive suggestions and arguments, through general and specialised language models, now being increasingly deployed in legal practice.

AI.tldr: AI and Law research approaches legal interpretation through three main methodologies: expert systems for knowledge engineering, argumentation frameworks for dialectical analysis, and machine learning for automated interpretation generation.
AI.motivation: To explore how AI and Law research has engaged with legal interpretation across different methodological approaches, tracking the evolution from knowledge engineering to contemporary machine learning applications in legal practice.
AI.method: The paper analyzes three distinct approaches: (1) Expert systems focusing on legal knowledge engineering to transfer human interpretations into knowledge-bases; (2) Argumentation research representing interpretive argument structures and dialectical interactions within argumentation frameworks; (3) Machine learning using general and specialized language models for automated generation of interpretive suggestions and arguments.
AI.result: The analysis reveals a progression from rule-based expert systems to structured argumentation frameworks, culminating in contemporary machine learning approaches that are increasingly deployed in practical legal applications for generating interpretive content.
AI.conclusion: AI and Law research has developed diverse methodological approaches to legal interpretation, with current trends favoring machine learning techniques that leverage language models to generate interpretive suggestions, representing a shift from knowledge representation to automated interpretation generation in legal practice.

title: Judge Reliability Harness: Stress Testing the Reliability of LLM Judges
comment: Accepted at Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond Workshop at ICLR 2026 - April 26, 2026, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
summary: We present the Judge Reliability Harness, an open source library for constructing validation suites that test the reliability of LLM judges. As LLM based scoring is widely deployed in AI benchmarks, more tooling is needed to efficiently assess the reliability of these methods. Given a benchmark dataset and an LLM judge configuration, the harness generates reliability tests that evaluate both binary judgment accuracy and ordinal grading performance for free-response and agentic task formats. We evaluate four state-of-the-art judges across four benchmarks spanning safety, persuasion, misuse, and agentic behavior, and find meaningful variation in performance across models and perturbation types, highlighting opportunities to improve the robustness of LLM judges. No judge that we evaluated is uniformly reliable across benchmarks using our harness. For example, our preliminary experiments on judges revealed consistency issues as measured by accuracy in judging another LLM's ability to complete a task due to simple text formatting changes, paraphrasing, changes in verbosity, and flipping the ground truth label in LLM-produced responses. The code for this tool is available at: https://github.com/RANDCorporation/judge-reliability-harness

AI.tldr: The Judge Reliability Harness is an open-source library for testing LLM judge reliability across benchmarks, revealing significant performance variations and consistency issues in current LLM-based scoring methods.
AI.motivation: LLM-based scoring is widely deployed in AI benchmarks, but there's insufficient tooling to efficiently assess the reliability of these methods. Current LLM judges need systematic evaluation for robustness and consistency across different task formats and perturbations.
AI.method: The harness generates reliability tests that evaluate both binary judgment accuracy and ordinal grading performance for free-response and agentic task formats. Given a benchmark dataset and LLM judge configuration, it systematically tests judges across various perturbation types including text formatting changes, paraphrasing, verbosity changes, and ground truth label flipping.
AI.result: Evaluation of four state-of-the-art judges across four benchmarks (safety, persuasion, misuse, and agentic behavior) revealed meaningful variation in performance across models and perturbation types. No judge was uniformly reliable across benchmarks, and preliminary experiments showed consistency issues due to simple text perturbations.
AI.conclusion: The Judge Reliability Harness provides essential tooling for assessing LLM judge reliability, highlighting significant opportunities to improve robustness in LLM-based scoring methods. The open-source availability enables broader adoption and systematic evaluation of judge reliability in AI benchmarks.

title: Dissociating Direct Access from Inference in AI Introspection
summary: Introspection is a foundational cognitive ability, but its mechanism is not well understood. Recent work has shown that AI models can introspect. We study their mechanism of introspection, first extensively replicating Lindsey et al. (2025)'s thought injection detection paradigm in large open-source models. We show that these models detect injected representations via two separable mechanisms: (i) probability-matching (inferring from perceived anomaly of the prompt) and (ii) direct access to internal states. The direct access mechanism is content-agnostic: models detect that an anomaly occurred but cannot reliably identify its semantic content. The two model classes we study confabulate injected concepts that are high-frequency and concrete (e.g., "apple'"); for them correct concept guesses typically require significantly more tokens. This content-agnostic introspective mechanism is consistent with leading theories in philosophy and psychology.

AI.tldr: AI models detect thought injections via two mechanisms: probability-matching (inferring from prompt anomalies) and direct access to internal states (content-agnostic anomaly detection). Models confabulate high-frequency concrete concepts and need more tokens for correct concept identification.
AI.motivation: To understand the mechanism of introspection in AI models, particularly how they detect injected representations, building on recent work showing AI models can introspect.
AI.method: Extensive replication of Lindsey et al. (2025)'s thought injection detection paradigm in large open-source models, analyzing detection mechanisms through probability-matching and direct access to internal states.
AI.result: Models detect injected representations via two separable mechanisms: probability-matching (inferring from perceived prompt anomalies) and direct access to internal states (content-agnostic anomaly detection). Models confabulate high-frequency concrete concepts like "apple" and require significantly more tokens for correct concept guesses.
AI.conclusion: The content-agnostic introspective mechanism (direct access to internal states) aligns with leading theories in philosophy and psychology, providing insight into how AI models perform introspection.

title: Distributed Partial Information Puzzles: Examining Common Ground Construction Under Epistemic Asymmetry
summary: Establishing common ground, a shared set of beliefs and mutually recognized facts, is fundamental to collaboration, yet remains a challenge for current AI systems, especially in multimodal, multiparty settings, where the collaborators bring different information to the table. We introduce the Distributed Partial Information Puzzle (DPIP), a collaborative construction task that elicits rich multimodal communication under epistemic asymmetry. We present a multimodal dataset of these interactions, annotated and temporally aligned across speech, gesture, and action modalities to support reasoning over propositional content and belief dynamics. We then evaluate two paradigms for modeling common ground (CG): (1) state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), prompted to infer shared beliefs from multimodal updates, and (2) an axiomatic pipeline grounded in Dynamic Epistemic Logic (DEL) that incrementally performs the same task. Results on the annotated DPIP data indicate that it poses a challenge to modern LLMs' abilities to track both task progression and belief state.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DPIP, a collaborative construction task that tests AI systems' ability to establish common ground in multimodal, multiparty settings with information asymmetry, and evaluates LLMs vs. logic-based approaches on this challenge.
AI.motivation: Current AI systems struggle with establishing common ground (shared beliefs and mutually recognized facts) in collaborative multimodal, multiparty settings where participants have different information (epistemic asymmetry). There's a need for tasks that elicit rich multimodal communication and test AI's ability to reason about belief dynamics.
AI.method: 1) Introduced Distributed Partial Information Puzzle (DPIP), a collaborative construction task designed to elicit multimodal communication under epistemic asymmetry. 2) Created a multimodal dataset of these interactions with temporal alignment across speech, gesture, and action modalities. 3) Evaluated two modeling paradigms: a) state-of-the-art LLMs prompted to infer shared beliefs from multimodal updates, and b) an axiomatic pipeline based on Dynamic Epistemic Logic (DEL) that incrementally performs belief tracking.
AI.result: DPIP poses a significant challenge to modern LLMs' abilities to track both task progression and belief state. The annotated dataset reveals limitations in current AI systems' capacity to reason over propositional content and belief dynamics in multimodal collaborative settings.
AI.conclusion: Establishing common ground in multimodal, multiparty settings remains a challenging problem for AI systems. The DPIP task and dataset provide a valuable benchmark for evaluating approaches to belief tracking and common ground establishment, highlighting the limitations of current LLM-based methods compared to formal logic-based approaches.

title: Towards Provably Unbiased LLM Judges via Bias-Bounded Evaluation
summary: As AI models progress beyond simple chatbots into more complex workflows, we draw ever closer to the event horizon beyond which AI systems will be utilized in autonomous, self-maintaining feedback loops. Any autonomous AI system will depend on automated, verifiable rewards and feedback; in settings where ground truth is sparse or non-deterministic, one practical source of such rewards is an LLM-as-a-Judge. Although LLM judges continue to improve, the literature has yet to introduce systems capable of enforcing standards with strong guarantees, particularly when bias vectors are unknown or adversarially discovered. To remedy this issue, we propose average bias-boundedness (A-BB), an algorithmic framework which formally guarantees reductions of harm/impact as a result of any measurable bias in an LLM judge. Evaluating on Arena-Hard-Auto with four LLM judges, we achieve (tau=0.5, delta=0.01) bias-bounded guarantees while retaining 61-99% correlation with original rankings across formatting and schematic bias settings, with most judge-bias combinations exceeding 80%. The code to reproduce our findings is available at https://github.com/penfever/bias-bounded-evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Average Bias-Boundedness (A-BB), a framework that provides formal guarantees for reducing harm from measurable biases in LLM-as-a-Judge systems, achieving strong bias-bounded guarantees while maintaining high correlation with original rankings.
AI.motivation: As AI systems move toward autonomous, self-maintaining feedback loops, they require automated, verifiable rewards and feedback. LLM-as-a-Judge systems are practical sources for such rewards, but current systems lack strong guarantees against biases, especially when bias vectors are unknown or adversarially discovered.
AI.method: The paper proposes Average Bias-Boundedness (A-BB), an algorithmic framework that formally guarantees reductions of harm/impact from any measurable bias in an LLM judge. The method evaluates on Arena-Hard-Auto with four different LLM judges.
AI.result: The framework achieves (tau=0.5, delta=0.01) bias-bounded guarantees while retaining 61-99% correlation with original rankings across formatting and schematic bias settings. Most judge-bias combinations exceed 80% correlation with original rankings.
AI.conclusion: The A-BB framework provides a practical solution for enforcing standards with strong guarantees against biases in LLM-as-a-Judge systems, addressing a critical gap in the literature as AI systems become more autonomous and dependent on automated feedback mechanisms.

title: The Spike, the Sparse and the Sink: Anatomy of Massive Activations and Attention Sinks
summary: We study two recurring phenomena in Transformer language models: massive activations, in which a small number of tokens exhibit extreme outliers in a few channels, and attention sinks, in which certain tokens attract disproportionate attention mass regardless of semantic relevance. Prior work observes that these phenomena frequently co-occur and often involve the same tokens, but their functional roles and causal relationship remain unclear. Through systematic experiments, we show that the co-occurrence is largely an architectural artifact of modern Transformer design, and that the two phenomena serve related but distinct functions. Massive activations operate globally: they induce near-constant hidden representations that persist across layers, effectively functioning as implicit parameters of the model. Attention sinks operate locally: they modulate attention outputs across heads and bias individual heads toward short-range dependencies. We identify the pre-norm configuration as the key choice that enables the co-occurrence, and show that ablating it causes the two phenomena to decouple.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the relationship between massive activations and attention sinks in Transformers, showing they are architectural artifacts that serve distinct functions but co-occur due to pre-norm design.
AI.motivation: To understand the functional roles and causal relationship between two recurring phenomena in Transformer language models: massive activations (extreme outliers in few channels) and attention sinks (tokens attracting disproportionate attention mass).
AI.method: Systematic experiments analyzing Transformer architectures, particularly focusing on the pre-norm configuration, and performing ablation studies to decouple the phenomena.
AI.result: Massive activations operate globally by inducing near-constant hidden representations across layers (implicit parameters), while attention sinks operate locally by modulating attention outputs and biasing heads toward short-range dependencies. The co-occurrence is largely an architectural artifact enabled by pre-norm configuration.
AI.conclusion: Massive activations and attention sinks serve related but distinct functions, and their frequent co-occurrence is an artifact of modern Transformer design rather than a necessary functional coupling.
